    Instructor Notes

    This page is for the people running the workshop. It covers what to prepare, a run-sheet for each day, the solutions and how to rescue someone who is stuck, and how to maintain the lesson. Each episode also has an Instructor view box with its own timings, common problems and a bridge to the next episode.

    Before the workshop

    About a week before

    • BASH 

      cd build/peakfinder
git remote add origin <the public course repository URL>
git push origin main background-subtraction colleague/normalise-modes untangle --tags

      The repository must be public (so learners can fork it). Then put its URL in learners/setup.md.

    If you don’t use rebase yourself yet. Many instructors don’t, and that’s fine. Before teaching it, do the exercises in episodes 5, 6 and 7 once on your own computer (about an hour), and practise the rescue commands. Everything in the lesson is safe, because of the backup branch and the reflog.

    Day 1 run-sheet

    Times assume a 09:00 start and a 15-minute break after episode 4. They come from each episode’s own “teaching + exercises” times, so they leave about 44 minutes of slack (end 12:16). Follow-along sessions usually run over by a third, so treat the slack as spent.

    Start Episode Check before moving on If you’re behind, cut
    09:00 01 Welcome and the Story (15 min) Everyone is on main with a clean git status; git branch -r shows the other branches and git tag shows v0.1.0 and v0.2.0; pytest passes; git push works; partners are collaborators on each other’s forks. Shorten the collaborator-invite walkthrough (email it beforehand).
    09:15 02 A Mental Model: Snapshots and Labels (22 min) Nothing to check. Ask: “what does a branch point at?” Skip the git hash-object check.
    09:37 03 Planning and Atomic Commits (23 min) Everyone has written down their list of commits. They need it for episode 6. Collapse the prefixes callout; shorten the example.
    10:00 04 The Safety Net: Reflog (15 min) Everyone ends on main with a clean git status (no leftover experiment branch or README edits). Skip the knowledge check.
    10:30 break back (15 min)
    10:30 05 Shaping a Commit: Staging, Amend, Reset and Restore (27 min) The untangle branch has two new commits (--title, then the markers), no DEBUG print, and pytest passes. Skip the git add -p callout and the reset knowledge check.
    10:57 06 Interactive Rebase: Rewriting a Messy Branch (43 min) background-subtraction has seven clean commits; main is unchanged and nobody merged the branch. Don’t cut. If behind, give out the finished todo from the solution earlier.
    11:40 07 The Daily Loop: Fixup and Autosquash (36 min) A feature branch (feature-prominence or feature-widths) is pushed to the fork, with three clean commits and no fixup!; main is unchanged. Learners watch the short demo instead of typing it.

    Day 2 run-sheet

    A 15-minute break after episode 11. End 12:15, leaving about 45 minutes of slack.

    Start Episode Check before moving on If you’re behind, cut
    09:00 08 Day 2 Recap and Warm-up (9 min) State check passed: clean tree, feature branch present on the fork. Standing rules said aloud (own fork; Rebase and merge). Skip the quiz; do the state check only.
    09:09 09 Rebase vs Merge, and Resolving Conflicts (35 min) Feature rebased onto main (straight line), pushed with --force-with-lease, and one test still fails (the colleague’s). Nobody typed the merge demo. Skip the merge demo (the diagrams show the double back).
    09:44 10 Tracking Down a Bug: Blame and Bisect (30 min) The fix is on main (fast-forwarded and pushed), the feature is rebased onto it, and all tests pass. Skip the by-hand bisect demo, then the log -S/-L callout.
    10:14 11 Pull Requests: Authoring and Reviewing (30 min) A pull request is open on the learner’s own fork (not the course repo), reviewed by the partner, and a fixup pushed. Finishing is optional. Skip the Finishing section (squash and merge).
    10:59 break back (15 min)
    10:59 12 Catching Problems Early: Shift Left and CI (26 min) Actions enabled; the add-ci pull request has gone green, then red, then green again (or the fallback demo has been shown). Do the exercise as a demo, or use the fallback.
    11:25 13 Releases: Versions, Tags and Cherry-pick (35 min) release/0.2 and tag v0.2.1 pushed, with the fix cherry-picked. Skip the optional GitHub release.
    12:00 14 Tooling and Wrap-up (15 min) Each person has named one habit to try. Read-afterwards: do only the take-aways.

    The standing rules for day 2 (said once, in episode 8): every pull request is on the learner’s own fork, and you merge with Rebase and merge.

    Solutions

    Every exercise has a solution box in the episode. The ones people most often need:

    Exercise Where the answer is End state to check
    03 smell test the solution box (a 7-commit list) learners wrote their own list
    05 untangle the solution box (VS Code and command line) git log --oneline -3 shows two new commits; git grep DEBUG is empty
    06 rebase 1 and 2 the solution boxes give the finished todo lists git log --oneline main.. shows seven commits; git diff --stat backup/background-subtraction shows only scratch_smoothing.py
    07 features A/B the solution box three commits, no fixup!, pytest passes
    09 rebase and conflict the solution box gives the resolved find_peaks for A and B straight line, one failing test left
    10 the fix the solution box pytest passes after the second rebase
    12 CI the solution box, and the workflow file in the episode green, red, then green
    13 release the solution box tag v0.2.1 on release/0.2

    Rescuing someone who is stuck

    First, the general tools, which cover most problems:

    • git status says what git thinks is happening and what to do next.
    • git rebase --abort (or git merge --abort, git cherry-pick --abort) puts everything back.
    • git reflog finds a lost commit (episode 4).
    • git reset --hard origin/<branch> puts a branch back to what’s on their fork. Use it with care: it throws away local changes.

    For specific exercises, helpers need the solutions repository as a remote:

    BASH 

    git remote add solutions <the private solutions repository URL>
git fetch solutions
    Problem Rescue
    Episode 6: badly tangled, no backup git switch -C background-subtraction origin/background-subtraction starts again from the messy branch. Or, to give them the finished branch: git switch -C background-subtraction solutions/solution/background-subtraction
    Episode 7: a lost feature branch git switch -C feature-prominence solutions/solution/feature-prominence (or feature-widths)
    Episode 9: stuck in the conflict git rebase --abort, then redo it, pasting the resolved find_peaks from the episode’s solution box
    Episode 10: missed the fix git switch main, then git cherry-pick solutions/solution/fix-normalise
    Their main has stray commits git switch main, then git reset --hard origin/main (check origin/main is the right one)
    No tags in their fork They ticked “Copy the default branch only”. Re-fork with it unticked, or git fetch <original repository URL> --tags
    Pull request opened against the course repository Close it, and open it again on their own fork

    Online delivery

    • Put people in pairs in breakout rooms for the exercises, and have helpers visit the rooms. Create the rooms before you need them, and keep a list of who is with whom.
    • Share your VS Code with the terminal visible, at a large font, as people follow your commands.
    • Use the chat for “done” reactions after each step, so you can see who is behind without stopping.
    • Pairs that lose a partner can review the prepared pull request (episode 11) and follow the prepared Actions run (episode 12).

    Looking after the lesson

    • Rebuild the example repository with python tools/build_starter.py --force. It checks that the tests pass and fail where the episodes expect, that the example features conflict with the colleague’s work, and that the fix cherry-picks cleanly.
    • Any change under tools/ changes every commit hash, even a name or a date. After a rebuild, run python tools/remap_hashes.py <old hashes file> to update the hashes quoted in the episodes (the steps are in its docstring).
    • Check the diagrams with node tools/check_diagrams/check.mjs (add --render <folder> to draw images). It needs npm install once.
    • Check the lesson with sandpaper::validate_lesson(".") in R, and preview it with sandpaper::serve().

    Welcome and the Story

    Instructor Note

    Timing. 10 minutes talking, 5 for the discussion. If the setup check turns up problems, give helpers the stragglers and keep going. Don’t let the whole room wait for one laptop.

    The hook. Put the two logs up side by side. Don’t tell people which is “right”. Let them say it. Then say “The code is identical.” That is the idea of the whole workshop.

    Noisy plot. Make sure everyone has seen the 71. In episode 7 they’ll write a feature to fix it, and it helps them to care.

    Collaborator invitations. This is where people get stuck: the invitation sits in an email, and the invitee must accept. Check that pairs have done it now. On day 2, PR review needs it.

    Common setup problems (see the setup page for fixes):

    • forked with “Copy the main branch only” ticked (so only main, no tags): delete the fork and fork again
    • no way to git push (authentication)
    • core.editor not set, so the rebase editor will be vim
    • virtual environment not active, so pytest is not found

    Online. Drop the list of pairs in the chat, and create the breakout rooms before they’re needed. Have a helper in every room if possible.

    Pairs with an odd number. A trio works: one person is the reviewer for the next.


    A Mental Model: Snapshots and Labels

    Instructor Note

    Keep this brisk (about 25 minutes). The goal is a useful model, not a complete one, and people may ask about trees, blobs or packfiles. Park those and point them at the extras. If you want a deeper treatment (optional, end of day 2, or the learner reference), the deep dive is: objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags), content addressing, git hash-object, .git/objects.

    Likely questions:

    • “So git doesn’t store diffs?” Conceptually it stores snapshots. Under the hood it is clever about storing them compactly (packfiles), but you don’t need to care.
    • “What if two commits have the same content?” Different parents or timestamps mean different hashes.
    • “Can I see the old commit later?” Yes, that’s the next-but-one episode (reflog).

    Planning and Atomic Commits

    Instructor Note

    Timing: about 15 minutes of talk and 10 for the challenge. The challenge is reading only, in pairs, and we reuse the plan in episode 6. Keep it light: don’t spend long on commit message conventions, people have strong opinions and it is a rabbit hole. Show the table of “weak vs better” and move on.

    Possible discussion points:

    • “Should tests go in the same commit as the code?” There are two schools of thought. Our view: yes, if a commit changes behaviour, the test for it belongs with it, so every commit stands alone. But a separate test commit is fine, and our messy branch has one.
    • “This is too much work.” Answer: you will write less time worth of commit message than you save in review. And episodes 5 to 7 show how to get there without planning perfectly.
    • “What about squash merging? Doesn’t that make this pointless?” Squash is a good fallback when a branch has not been curated, but it throws away exactly the story we’re trying to tell. We’ll come back to this in episode 9.

    Make sure everyone writes the plan down (a text file or paper). They’ll need it in episode 6.


    The Safety Net: Reflog

    Instructor Note

    Pacing. This episode is the follow-along: learners type every step with you, so go slowly and pause after each command until people have caught up. There’s no separate challenge. If someone falls behind, they can watch and catch up at the knowledge check.

    Do the “oh no” moments as a live demo with everyone following. The drama is the point: say “I’ve lost all my work!” and pause before looking at the reflog.

    Cleanup: make sure everyone ends the episode with main checked out, and with a clean git status. A bad README.md change left on main would cause confusing conflicts later. If anyone committed to main by mistake: git reset --hard origin/main (they have a fork, so it will be at the right place).

    VS Code has no built-in reflog view. (The GitLens extension adds one.) This is a terminal job.

    Common problems:

    • The reflog opens in a pager and people don’t know how to leave. It’s q.
    • Someone runs git reset --hard with uncommitted work, and asks about it. Use it as the live demonstration of “what the reflog can’t save”.

    Shaping a Commit: Staging, Amend, Reset and Restore

    Instructor Note

    Demo first (about 5 minutes). Do the first hunk of the challenge live in VS Code, so people see Stage Selected Ranges working: undo the commit, stage the lines about --title in cli.py, and show the file in both the Staged and the Changes lists. Then leave the rest to them.

    Things that go wrong:

    • “Stage Selected Ranges” is greyed out. They selected lines in the left (old) side of the diff or nothing at all. It has to be the right-hand side.
    • They stage the whole file by clicking +. They can unstage it again with -, or Unstage Selected Ranges for a part.
    • They commit the debug print and then need to remove it. Fine: it’s a chance to show git commit --amend, or git reset HEAD^ and again.
    • They discard something they wanted with Revert Selected Ranges. If it was committed, the reflog has it. If not, it’s gone. Use it as a reminder of episode 4.
    • VS Code shows no ... menu or Amend option: an older VS Code. Use the command line.

    Don’t skip the debrief (3 minutes). Ask: “How did you decide which lines go in which commit?” The answer, “by the idea they belong to”, is the skill.

    The untangle branch is built by tools/build_starter.py, and is the same for everyone.


    Interactive Rebase: Rewriting a Messy Branch

    Instructor Note

    Pause here until everyone has five commits. The commonest problems are:

    • The editor opened in vim (not VS Code), so core.editor wasn’t set. Fix it with git config --global core.editor "code --wait". If they are stuck in vim: :q! aborts the rebase step.
    • Typing in the wrong order. Remember it’s oldest first.
    • Saving the file but not closing the VS Code tab. Git waits until the tab is closed.
    • A commit moved above one that touches the same file, and a conflict. They can git rebase --abort and start again, with the todo list given in the solution.

    Instructor Note

    Give people about 10 to 12 minutes, then review it together. Live-demo the solution in the VS Code terminal while someone describes what they did.

    Make sure nobody merges background-subtraction into main at the end. Tomorrow, main has to be unchanged so that the colleague’s branch can be fast-forwarded onto it (episode 9). If anyone does, git reset --hard origin/main on main puts it right.

    Things that commonly go wrong:

    • Forgetting git rebase --continue after the split. git status says “interactive rebase in progress”.
    • git reset --hard instead of git reset. The changes are gone from the working directory! Show them how to recover: git rebase --abort, then start rebase 2 again.
    • Staged everything in one go, ending with a single commit again. Check with git show --stat.
    • A conflict in a reword step. This shouldn’t happen in this exercise. If it does, git rebase --abort and restart.
    • Someone who is hopelessly lost: have them git rebase --abort (if in a rebase), then git reset --hard backup/background-subtraction, and go again from rebase 1. If they have no backup, a helper can give them the clean result (see the instructor guide for the rescue commands).

    The Daily Loop: Fixup and Autosquash

    Instructor Note

    Demo (about 8 minutes, with learners following). It’s deliberately short: two commits, one docstring fixup, and the autosquash. People copy the code from the page, so the demo is about the git. The key moments to slow down for:

    1. Spotting the missing docstring, and the thought “this belongs to commit 1, not a new commit.” Say it out loud.
    2. The fixup! commit at the end of the log, then the todo list with the fixup line already moved up under its commit. Pause here. People find this a pleasant surprise.
    3. The log afterwards: no fixup, nothing to hide.

    Save the time for the challenge, where they do it all themselves (and meet a bug that a test catches).

    Challenge (28 minutes). Pairs: each person works alone on their own computer, but can ask the other. Online: breakout rooms of two.

    Common problems:

    • git commit --fixup with a wrong hash (or a hash from before an earlier rebase). git log --oneline main.. and try again. If the fixup is wrong, git reset --soft HEAD^ and redo it.
    • The test doesn’t fail. They fixed the bug while writing the helper. Tell them to paste the code exactly as written.
    • B: only one >= fixed. The test still fails. Both loops need changing.
    • Autosquash doesn’t reorder anything. They ran git rebase main without -i (no autosquash), or the rebase.autoSquash setting is missing. Use git rebase -i --autosquash main.
    • Editor doesn’t open or hangs. core.editor isn’t code --wait (see setup).
    • A conflict during autosquash. Rare here. git rebase --abort, and check the fixup only touches the lines it should.

    Pushing: git push needs authentication to work, which was part of the setup. If someone’s push fails, pair them with a helper rather than losing time. They can still finish the exercise locally, and push later.

    End of day 1. Before finishing, check everyone has:

    • a pushed branch (feature-prominence or feature-widths) on their fork
    • main unchanged, and a clean git status

    Preview day 2: “Overnight, a colleague’s pull request gets merged into main. It touches the same function as yours…”


    Day 2 Recap and Warm-up

    Instructor Note

    Keep this to about 10 minutes. The quiz can be done by a show of hands, or by cold-calling. Don’t let it turn into a lecture.

    State check. The point is to find the people with a broken day-1 state before they hit episode 9. Common problems:

    • main has local commits, because they committed to it by mistake. git reset --hard origin/main fixes it.
    • The feature branch still contains fixup! commits, so they never ran the autosquash. They can do it now: git rebase -i --autosquash main.
    • They never pushed. git push.
    • The fork is missing the colleague’s branch (they forked with the default-branch-only option). Tomorrow’s story needs colleague/normalise-modes. They can fetch it from the original repository (git remote add upstream <url>, git fetch upstream) and push it to their fork, but it’s often quicker to re-fork.

    Fallback branches. Have a ready-made feature-prominence and feature-widths available for anyone who lost theirs. These aren’t published to the learners’ forks, so give the helpers a way to hand them out.


    Rebase vs Merge, and Resolving Conflicts

    Instructor Note

    Plan (about 35 minutes). Roughly: 10 minutes of explanation with the diagrams, 5 to fast-forward main, 5 for your demonstration of the merge (conflict, merge editor, graph, undo), 8 for the rebase challenge on their own, and 5 for the push and the buttons. The merge is a demo: learners watch and don’t type, so they resolve the conflict once, themselves, in the rebase. If you’re running short, skip the demo: the diagram already shows the double back.

    The demo is where you teach the merge editor. Open it, explain the three panes, and say out loud “which side has the colleague’s change, and which has mine?” before clicking anything. Then they do the same, alone, in the rebase.

    Roles swap in a rebase. Current and Incoming mean the opposite of merge. This catches everyone out. Spend a minute on the callout.

    Common problems:

    • They click “Accept Current” or “Accept Incoming” on a whole conflict and lose half of what they wanted. Check that the result has both Peak(...) and their new option (git diff main should show their feature). pytest will also fail with a NameError or TypeError.
    • They leave the markers in (<<<<<<<). git diff --check finds them.
    • They forget git rebase --continue: git status says “rebase in progress”.
    • An editor tab opens after --continue (it’s the commit message). Tell them to close the tab. If the editor isn’t set, they get vim; see the setup page.
    • They run git pull after being told not to: have them git reflog and reset, as in episode 4. A good chance to show it working.
    • They use --force rather than --force-with-lease. Remind them.
    • git merge --ff-only refuses: their main has commits of its own. git reset --hard origin/main first (then redo the fast-forward).
    • The one failing test after the rebase isn’t a mistake: it is the hook for episode 10. Don’t explain it yet.

    If someone is hopelessly stuck: git rebase --abort, and give them the resolved peaks.py from the solution, or have a helper pair with them.

    Bridge to episode 10: “We have one failing test, and it isn’t in our code. What changed?”


    Tracking Down a Bug: Blame and Bisect

    Instructor Note

    Plan (about 30 minutes). Roughly: 3 for the failing test and blame, 7 for bisect (you explain and show the by-hand version, then they run bisect run), 15 for the fix, merge and rebase. If it runs long, trim in this order: the by-hand demo, the -S/-L callout, then the Knowledge check.

    Bisect has two layers. Show the by-hand version once, briefly, so the idea of “binary search” lands. Then learners only type the three-line bisect run, which takes seconds.

    No pull request here, by design. The fix goes straight into main with a fast-forward, which keeps this episode short and saves the pull request mechanics for episode 11. Say out loud that a real team would open one.

    Common problems:

    • git bisect refuses, because of uncommitted changes. Stash or commit.
    • They forget git bisect reset, and wonder why they’re on a detached HEAD. git bisect reset fixes it.
    • They give git the arguments the wrong way round (git bisect start v0.1.0 main): bad first, then good. The result will be nonsense. git bisect reset and again.
    • Bisecting the whole test suite rather than tests/test_normalise.py: other failures can confuse it.
    • No v0.1.0 tag. Their fork has no tags. git tag shows what’s there. They can fetch tags from the original repository, or pair up.
    • git merge --ff-only refuses. main has moved, or they committed the fix on the wrong branch. git status, git log --oneline --graph, and check they branched from main.
    • git branch -d fix/normalise fails with “not fully merged”. The merge didn’t happen, or they’re on the wrong branch.
    • A conflict in the second rebase: it shouldn’t happen. It means they changed normalise.py in their feature branch.

    Bridge to episode 11: “Your feature is ready, on top of a working main. Time to ask your partner to review it.”


    Pull Requests: Authoring and Reviewing

    Instructor Note

    Timing (about 30 minutes). 12 minutes of talk, then the exercises in time-boxes: open the pull request (4), review (8), respond and approve (6). Use a visible timer. Review takes longest, so don’t let it overrun: three comments only. The Finishing section (squash and merge) is optional in the session: say it’s there for when they have time, or to do later. (Learners who don’t merge won’t be affected: nothing in the later episodes needs this feature merged.)

    The base repository trap. Check screens as people open their pull requests. Anything opened against the course repository should be closed and re-opened on the fork.

    Pairs. Make sure each learner has been added as a collaborator (episode 1), and the invitation accepted: they need it to be asked for a review. If a partner is missing or behind, pair them with a helper, or have them review the instructor’s example pull request.

    Online. Breakout rooms of two. Ask people to share the pull request link in the chat or room.

    Common problems:

    • The pull request is against the course repository. Close it and open a new one on the fork.
    • The reviewer can’t find the pull request. Send the link. Check notification emails.
    • They git commit --fixup the wrong commit. The autosquash puts the change in the wrong place. git rebase --abort, or fix it with another interactive rebase.
    • They squash before the reviewer has looked and then wonder where their comments went. GitHub keeps them, marked “outdated”.
    • No partner. Use the prepared example pull request. Have one ready on your own fork, with a few things to comment on.
    • git diff @{u} HEAD isn’t empty. Something else changed. Look at it with git diff @{u} HEAD --stat.
    • @{u} means nothing, or errors: the branch has no upstream. git push -u origin <branch> sets it.
    • @{u} in some shells needs quoting ('@{u}'). In Git Bash it works as is.
    • After merging, the branch still shows in the list. There is a Delete branch button on the merged pull request.

    What to point out: that every commit and every comment they wrote on day 1 and now is the thing the reviewer is reading. A reviewer who can follow the story approves faster.


    Catching Problems Early: Shift Left and CI

    Instructor Note

    Timing (about 26 minutes). Talk for 10: the table of stages is the key idea, and the stage 2 and 3 sections can be quick. Then the single challenge, which has just one pull request for both exercises. Start the CI pull request early and talk while it runs: the first run takes up to a minute, and there’s waiting time in the exercise. If you’re short on time, do part 1 together, then do part 2 and 3 (break and fix) as a demonstration on your screen. The “going further” step is talking only.

    Emphasise the principle: push each check left until it’s too slow or annoying. Ask the room: “what do you already run before pushing?”

    Test this before the workshop. I could check the workflow with actionlint and its commands in a clean environment, but not run it on GitHub. Do the whole exercise on a real fork the day before. Also re-check the versions of actions/checkout and actions/setup-python.

    Actions must be enabled on each fork (setup page, step 6). Ask for a show of hands before you start. The Actions tab shows an enable button if not.

    Common problems:

    • Nothing happens on the pull request. Actions is disabled on the fork, or the file isn’t in .github/workflows/, or the pull request is on the course repository instead of the fork.
    • The workflow fails with a YAML error. Indentation, or a tab. Open the Actions tab and read the error.
    • “Rebase and merge” is greyed out. The branch isn’t up to date, or the repository setting is off. Check Settings then General then Pull Requests.
    • The test doesn’t fail in the break-and-fix. They renamed the string in the test as well. Start again.
    • After the autosquash the push is rejected: use --force-with-lease.

    Prepare a fallback before the session. Actions is the part most likely to slow the room down (it runs on GitHub, so you can’t control the timing). Have these ready:

    • A prepared fork with the add-ci pull request already open: a green run, and then the breaking commit with a red run, and a link to each. (Or screenshots of each stage if you can’t rely on the network.)
    • A decision made in advance about when to stop waiting. A sensible rule: if checks haven’t appeared after two minutes, you screenshare the prepared run and move on.
    • Three levels of fallback, from best to simplest: (1) learners run it themselves; (2) learners do the git steps, and you demonstrate the Actions results on your screen; (3) you explain and demonstrate everything, and learners just read the workflow file. Any of them still teaches the idea.

    Limits. Public repositories get free Actions minutes. If the fork is private, the allowance is limited. Forks of public repositories are public.

    Bridge to episode 13: “We have a fix, merged on main. But users are still running version 0.2, which has the bug. How do we get the fix to them?”


    Releases: Versions, Tags and Cherry-pick

    Instructor Note

    Timing (about 35 minutes). 15 minutes for the lifecycle, versions, tags and cherry-pick, and 20 for the exercise. The GitHub release is optional, and a good thing to demo while people finish.

    Keep the lifecycle simple. Don’t be drawn into branching-model debates. If someone asks about git flow, say it’s a heavier version of the same idea, for software with scheduled releases, and move on.

    Find the fix by its message. Learners deleted their fix/normalise branch in episode 10, so they look up the commit on main with git log --grep. (The hash is the same one the branch had, but they may not have noted it.)

    Common problems:

    • git cherry-pick says the commit is empty or already applied. They are on main instead of release/0.2. Check git branch --show-current.
    • git switch -c release/0.2 v0.2.0 says the tag doesn’t exist. Their fork has no tags (forked with “Copy the default branch only”). git tag shows what’s there. They can fetch tags from the original repository, or pair up.
    • They forget -x. Harmless here, but explain what it would have told them.
    • A conflict on the cherry-pick. It shouldn’t happen. If it does, they’ve probably edited normalise.py on the release branch. git cherry-pick --abort and start again.
    • They tag with a lightweight tag (no -a). It works, but git tag -n shows no message. Delete it (git tag -d v0.2.1) and re-tag.
    • The tag doesn’t appear on GitHub. They pushed the branch but not the tag. git push origin v0.2.1.
    • No “Create a new release” button. On a fork, check Releases is enabled under Settings.

    Bridge to episode 14: “That’s the whole workflow. A few things to make it quicker.”


    Tooling and Wrap-up

    Instructor Note

    This episode is a menu. It’s fine to skip most of it, or to tell people it’s there to read afterwards. If you do one thing, do the take-aways and the “one habit” challenge.

    The challenge is also a quiet way to end. Ask two or three people to share their chosen habit.

    Before you finish: point people to the reference page, remind them their forks and branches are theirs to keep, and share the feedback link.

    Optional extras for a longer session or a follow-up: how git stores files (objects, trees, packfiles), git bisect with a script on a bigger history, git rerere in action, worktrees as an exercise, and a look at a real project’s pull requests.
